sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Initial Diagnostic Dilemma: Sepsis vs. Thrombotic Microangiopathy
sections.description: This section details the patient's initial presentation following a dog bite, focusing on the classic signs of Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis complicated by Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC). It explores the clinical challenge of distinguishing between sepsis-induced organ failure and the early stages of Thrombotic Microangiopathy (TMA), emphasizing why Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS) was initially deemed unlikely due to the presence of leukopenia and normal haptoglobin.
subtopics: History of exposure: Dog bite and delay in antibiotic prophylaxis
Initial clinical triad: Septic shock, refractory hypoglycemia, and mottled extremities
Laboratory interpretation: Pancytopenia, coagulopathy, and metabolic acidosis in the context of DIC
Differential diagnosis at admission: Acute leukemia vs. Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) vs. Sepsis-induced TMA
The diagnostic pitfall: Why hemolysis markers were initially absent or masked by DIC

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Reasoning: Unmasking Complement-Mediated HUS After Sepsis Resolution
sections.description: This section analyzes the pivotal shift in the patient's clinical course where sepsis improved but isolated hemolysis and thrombocytopenia emerged. It walks through the systematic exclusion of other causes of TMA (TTP, STEC-HUS) and the specific laboratory findings that confirmed Complement-Mediated HUS (CM-HUS), including the interpretation of a false-positive Coombs test and the significance of ADAMTS13 levels.
subtopics: Temporal evolution: The transition from resolving DIC to isolated Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia (MAHA)
Ruling out Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP): Interpreting ADAMTS13 activity (>10%) and PLASMIC score
Excluding Shiga Toxin-E. coli HUS: Role of stool PCR and lack of prodromal diarrhea
Investigating Autoimmune Hemolysis: Understanding the false-positive Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT) in penicillin-treated patients
Renal Biopsy findings: Differentiating Acute Tubular Necrosis from fibrin thrombi and crescents indicative of TMA

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology: Infectious Triggers and Dysregulation of the Alternative Complement Pathway
sections.description: This section provides a focused review of the pathophysiology behind CM-HUS, specifically addressing how bacterial infections like C. canimorsus can act as 'triggers' for complement dysregulation. It clarifies why standard complement levels (C3/C4) may be normal during acute episodes and discusses the interplay between bacterial virulence factors (capsule), host defense mechanisms, and endothelial injury.
subtopics: Mechanism of CM-HUS: Uncontrolled activation of the alternative complement pathway
Genetic predisposition vs. acquired triggers: Analyzing this case's lack of identifiable germline mutations
The role of C. canimorsus in complement activation: Serum sensitivity versus capsule-mediated resistance
Why C3/C4 levels are often normal in acute CM-HUS events
Endothelial damage cascade leading to thrombus formation in glomerular capillaries

sections._content: Therapeutic Strategy: Bridging with Plasma Exchange and Targeted Eculizumab Therapy
sections._desc: This section examines the complex management decisions required when treating CM-HUS in a patient with recent bacteremia. It contrasts the roles of Plasma Exchange (PEX) as a temporizing measure versus Eculizumab as definitive therapy, addresses the critical safety dilemma of administering terminal complement inhibition during active infection risk, and outlines vaccination protocols.
subtopics: Plasma Exchange rationale in CM-HUS vs. TTP: Removing inflammatory mediators vs. replacing deficient enzymes
The timing dilemma: Initiating Eculizumab after clearing bacteremia to prevent overwhelming sepsis
Meningococcal vaccination requirements prior to or concurrent with complement blockade
Antibiotic prophylaxis strategies for patients on long-term eculizumab therapy
Monitoring response criteria: Return of diuresis and normalization of hematologic parameters

sections._content: Prognostic Factors, Long-Term Outcomes, and Clinical Lessons Learned
sections._desc: This concluding section synthesizes the patient's recovery trajectory, evaluates prognostic indicators such as time-to-treatment initiation, discusses genetic counseling implications when no mutation is found, and extracts key teaching points regarding rare zoonotic triggers for TMA.
subtopics: Impact of delayed Eculizumab initiation on renal recovery potential
Interpretation of negative genetic testing in infection-triggered CM-HUS cases
Long-term follow-up requirements for residual chronic kidney disease
Key takeaways for clinicians recognizing TMA masquerading as sepsis complications
The emerging association between Capnocytophaga canimorsus and complement-mediated disorders
